research_notes:
Which? 23 Sep 2022: Epson WF-3820 ink £1.78/ml vs Dom Perignon 24p/ml (>7x); set £111.99; 3 sets/yr >£330 vs <£140 third-party; only 4% of inkjet owners found third-party didn't work; asked CMA to investigate branded ink pricing and HP dynamic security; HP: 'Dynamic security is a process that authenticates print supplies' (quality, IP, counterfeits); Epson doesn't block via firmware; Brother accepts third-party.
Which? 28 Sep 2026: Canon Pixma TS9551Ca, 30 pages/month, 10 yrs: original £762 vs third-party £321; HP+ blocks third-party ink entirely, opt-in irreversible.
HP FY2025 (8-K Q4): revenue $55,295M; Printing $16,702M, op earnings $3,118M, margin 18.7%; Personal Systems $38,532M, earnings $2,054M, margin 5.3%; Supplies $10,916M (65% of printing). Printing = 30% of revenue, 60% of the two segments' op earnings (my calc).
Lores CNBC Jan 2024 (The Register 19 Jan 2024): 'bad investment' quote; 'make printing a subscription'; 'embed viruses into cartridges'; HP bug bounty Oct 2022 confirmed reprogrammable third-party chips could deliver malware.
ThinkJet 1984, $495 (~$1,478 today), cartridges $8, ~500 pages (TechRadar).
Fortune 7 Oct 2019: shares -9.6%; 7,000-9,000 job cuts; two printer categories (cheaper locked to HP ink vs pricier unlocked); Argus analyst Kelleher on online cartridge buying; ~65% of printing revenue from supplies.
13 Sep 2016 firmware: cartridges rejected, 'damaged or missing' messages HP admitted were wrong; US settlement $1.5M (The Register Sep 2018).
ACCC 3 May 2018: ~220,000 printers, 10 OfficeJet models, $50 per blocked customer, HP admitted non-disclosure likely breached ACL.
AGCM 9 Dec 2020: €10M fine; limits not disclosed, changed by firmware updates; firmware recorded cartridge data, used to deny assistance; ordered packaging disclosure.
Instant Ink 13M+ subscribers (Lores, Mar 2024); Tran Oct 2023: profit-upfront and HP+ printers = 60% of unit shipments (The Register 7 Mar 2024).

plan.title: Why Printer Ink Costs More Than Champagne
alt_titles: HP Thinks You're a Bad Investment If You Buy Cheap Ink
How HP Really Makes Money (It's Not the Printers)
plan.description:
Some printer ink costs more than seven times as much as Dom Pérignon champagne. This is how HP really makes money from printer ink, why its printers block cheaper cartridges, what regulators in three countries found, and why I think ink is mostly a rip-off.

Why is printer ink so expensive? HP's printing business is under a third of its sales but about 60% of the profit from its two businesses, and supplies are about two thirds of printing revenue.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:45 The eight dollar cartridge
2:00 The real business
4:10 Locking the door
5:30 Caught
7:20 The subscription
8:30 The verdict

tags: why is printer ink so expensive

segments.narration: Why does printer ink cost more than champagne? That's not a joke. A consumer group actually measured it.
In 2022, the UK consumer group Which? priced a set of Epson ink at one pound seventy-eight per millilitre.
Dom Pérignon champagne worked out at twenty-four pence per millilitre. The ink was more than seven times the price.
And you've probably paid it. Maybe for a printer you used twice a month.
The company that sells the most of this stuff is HP. And its boss once said something on TV that explains the whole business.
If a customer doesn't use HP's supplies, he said, that customer is a bad investment.

visual.text: If that customer doesn't print enough or doesn't use our supplies, it's a *bad investment*.

segments.narration: A bad investment. That's you, if you buy cheaper ink.
And here's the strange part. HP sells far more computers than printers, yet printing makes it more profit. We'll get to how.
So is printer ink a rip-off? I think it is, mostly. By the end you'll see why, and what HP says in its defence.
To understand it, we have to go back to 1984, and an eight dollar cartridge.
That year, HP launched the ThinkJet, one of the first inkjet printers built for ordinary offices.
It cost four hundred and ninety-five dollars. About fifteen hundred in today's money.
Its cartridges cost eight dollars each and printed around five hundred pages.
Four years later, in 1988, came the DeskJet. Three hundred dots per inch, two pages a minute, and a sheet feeder. Inkjets were ready for everyone.
In 1991, colour arrived with the DeskJet 500C. Now you could run out of colour ink as well as black.
Notice the shape of that deal. You buy the machine once. You buy the ink forever.
Business schools call it the razor and blades model. Sell the handle cheaply, and make your money on the blades.
Printers turned out to be the perfect version of it. Every printer only takes its own cartridges, and every cartridge runs dry.
Over the next decades, inkjets moved from offices into almost every home. And the ink became a gold mine.
How big a gold mine? HP's own numbers tell you.
HP is really two businesses. It sells personal computers, and it sells printing.
In its 2025 financial year, HP brought in fifty-five point three billion dollars.
Computers were the big one: thirty-eight and a half billion. Printing brought in sixteen point seven.
So computers are the main business, right? Look at the profit.
Computers made about two point one billion dollars in operating profit. Printing made three point one billion.
Printing is less than a third of HP's sales. It's about sixty percent of the profit from those two businesses.
The margins show why. Every dollar of printing made almost nineteen cents of profit. Every dollar of computers made about five.
And inside printing, most of the money isn't printers. It's supplies: ink and toner. About ten point nine billion dollars of it.
That's roughly two thirds of the whole printing business.
And this isn't new. Back in 2019, printing's profit margin was fifteen point six percent, against five point six for computers. Nearly two thirds of printing revenue was already supplies.
Fortune described it as a razor and blades business, where the ink profits subsidise so much elsewhere in the company.

visual.text: ...*subsidize* so much elsewhere in the company.

segments.narration: So when Lores calls a customer an investment, he's being honest. The printer is the cost. The ink is the return.
Which raises an obvious problem. What if you buy your ink somewhere else?
Plenty of people do. Third-party cartridges can cost a fraction of the original.
In 2019, an analyst at Argus Research warned that more business customers were buying replacement cartridges online, eating into HP's most profitable business.
That October, HP's shares fell almost ten percent in a day, after it announced up to nine thousand job cuts and a rethink of its printer business.
HP employed about fifty-five thousand people at the time. Yet on the same day, it raised its dividend by ten percent and promised more share buybacks.
The plan was simple. A cheaper printer that only works with HP ink. Or a pricier one that takes any ink you like.
But HP had already been doing something else. Something buyers didn't know about.
On the thirteenth of September 2016, owners of some HP printers woke up to a problem.
Their printers suddenly refused cartridges that had worked the day before.
The error messages said the cartridges were damaged or missing. HP later admitted those messages were wrong.
The cartridges were fine. They just weren't made by HP.
An earlier firmware update had installed a feature HP calls Dynamic Security. It checks whether a cartridge is HP's own, and on many printers it refuses the rest.
A later lawsuit says HP had used Dynamic Security from around 2010.
Italy's regulator later described it the same way. Printers accept original HP cartridges, and refuse to print with non-original ones, or even with cartridges made before a certain date.
HP's explanation is that Dynamic Security authenticates supplies, to protect print quality and its intellectual property, and to stop counterfeits.

visual.text: Dynamic security is a process that *authenticates print supplies*.

segments.narration: Lores went further. He told CNBC that you can embed viruses into cartridges.

visual.text: We have seen that you can embed *viruses* into cartridges.

segments.narration: And he said it is important for HP to protect its intellectual property.
To be fair, there's something to that. HP's bug bounty program confirmed in 2022 that third-party cartridges with reprogrammable chips could deliver malware.
But critics point out that a printer that blocks cheaper ink also happens to protect HP's most profitable product. And regulators weren't convinced.
In May 2018, Australia's consumer watchdog, the ACCC, stepped in.
It said HP had sold around two hundred and twenty thousand printers there that could block non-HP cartridges, without telling buyers.
The ACCC's deputy chair put it simply: consumers were not made aware of the restriction on using non-HP ink cartridges.

visual.text: Consumers were *not made aware* of the restriction on using non-HP ink cartridges.
visual.who: Dr Michael Schaper, ACCC Deputy Chair

segments.narration: HP admitted that not disclosing it was likely to breach Australian consumer law. It agreed to pay fifty dollars to each customer who was blocked.
Ten OfficeJet models were affected. HP also promised a firmware update that removed the block from some of them.
In the US, owners sued. HP agreed to pay one and a half million dollars into a settlement fund for people whose printing was interrupted.
Then came Italy. In December 2020, the competition authority there fined HP ten million euros.
It found that HP didn't properly tell buyers about the limits on non-original cartridges, and that firmware updates changed those limits later, again without proper notice.
And there was more. The authority said HP's firmware quietly recorded which cartridges people used, original or not.
According to the regulator, that data was used to deny help to printers that had run non-original cartridges.
Italy ordered HP to say clearly on its packaging what each printer would and wouldn't accept.
HP appealed. A regional court in Lazio rejected the appeal, and the ten million euro fine stands.
Consumer groups in Italy, Belgium, Spain, Portugal and Brazil then demanded up to a hundred and fifty euros for each affected owner. That was a demand, not a court ruling.
In 2022, Which? asked Britain's competition regulator to investigate branded ink pricing, and HP's Dynamic Security in particular.
And it isn't over. In January 2024, a new US class action claimed that an HP update in late 2022 or early 2023 again disabled printers when a non-HP cartridge was put in.
The suit also claims HP raised its own cartridge prices in the same period. Those are allegations. Our sources show no ruling on them yet.
So what does an HP owner who wants cheaper ink actually do? Which? says that because of Dynamic Security, most HP printers need remanufactured cartridges: used HP shells, refilled.
Those cost more than third-party ink for other brands. But they're still usually much cheaper than original HP ink.
Not every brand blocks third-party ink. Epson told Which? it doesn't stop it through firmware. Brother said all its printers accept it.
Which tells you blocking isn't a law of nature. It's a choice.
So HP found a smoother way to keep you. Subscriptions.
Lores has said HP's long-term goal is to make printing a subscription.

visual.text: Our long-term objective is to make printing a *subscription*.

segments.narration: With Instant Ink, your printer tells HP when it's running low, and new cartridges arrive by post. You pay a monthly fee for a set number of pages.
By March 2024, it had more than thirteen million subscribers.
It needs your printer connected directly to the internet. And HP's own help page says Instant Ink cartridges won't work after the billing cycle in which you cancel.
Prices move, too. In January 2024, German subscribers were told the ten-page plan would go from ninety-nine cents to one forty-nine a month. About fifty percent more.
And in the US, an HP plan that bundles the printer itself charges up to two hundred and seventy dollars if you leave early.
In the UK, plans currently run from one pound seventy-nine a month for ten pages to about twenty-nine pounds for seven hundred.
HP's newer HP Plus printers go further still. According to Which?, they block third-party ink completely, and once you opt in, you can't undo it.
By late 2023, HP said these printers, together with ones priced for profit upfront, were sixty percent of the printers it shipped.
So the deal has quietly flipped. You used to buy a printer and choose your ink. Now, more and more, the ink chooses you.
So, is printer ink a rip-off?
Here's the fair case for HP. Printers are cheap up front because the ink pays for them. Without that, you'd pay much more for the machine.
HP even offers that choice. And security worries about hacked cartridges aren't made up.
But look at what the numbers say. Ink so expensive it beats champagne by the millilitre.

In that 2022 test, a set of original Epson cartridges cost one hundred and twelve pounds. Replace it three times a year and that's over three hundred and thirty. Three third-party sets came in under a hundred and forty.
Over ten years, Which? found a Canon printer user would pay seven hundred and sixty-two pounds for original ink, or about three hundred and twenty with recommended third-party ink.
It also found some third-party inks cost as little as a tenth of the original. Its best value suppliers averaged about sixty percent cheaper.

visual.label: Which? best-value third-party ink
visual.sub: some as low as 1/10 the price

segments.narration: And only four percent of inkjet owners it surveyed said a third-party cartridge didn't work.
Add three regulators and a settlement over hidden blocking, and a CEO who calls ink-shopping customers a bad investment.
My verdict: the printer isn't the product. You are. Your ink habit is what HP is really selling to its shareholders.
So before you buy a printer, check three things. Does it accept third-party ink? What does a page really cost? And can you opt out of the lock?
If you print a lot, compare laser and ink tank printers on cost per page. If you rarely print, the library might be cheapest of all.
Because the cheapest page is the one you print on your own terms.
And if you liked this, watch how airlines make more from your credit card than from flying. Same trick, different machine.
